reason: The text portrays Egyptian elite figures unfavorably throughout. Pharaoh is depicted as tyrannical and oppressive, enslaving the Israelites, stubbornly refusing Moses and Aaron's demands, and resisting God's will despite miraculous signs. His heart is hardened (by God or himself) against the Israelites' liberation. The Egyptian wise men and magicians (חרטומים) are shown attempting to replicate Aaron's miracles but are ultimately defeated—Aaron's staff consumes theirs. More broadly, Egyptian rulers and their system are portrayed as instruments of oppression and resistance to God. In contrast, the Israelite leaders (Moses and Aaron) are elevated as God's chosen representatives. The passage establishes a clear moral dichotomy where the Egyptian elite, particularly Pharaoh, represent an unfavorable force opposing God and enslaving His people.
